text: The course's explicit honesty checkpoint. Two eras, defined precisely, with a clear statement of exactly which one we're in.

NISQ hardware runs circuits with no error correction at all, or only small-scale, demonstration-level correction — not enough to suppress errors below what the raw circuit accumulates. This means NISQ-era algorithms have to be chosen to tolerate that reality: shallow circuits with few enough sequential gates, variational methods that lean on a classical computer, or algorithms whose output can be checked or post-selected classically. NISQ hardware isn't a smaller, worse version of a fault-tolerant computer running the same algorithms slower — it's a fundamentally different operating regime, suited to a narrower set of problems.

The fault-tolerant era, not yet reached for general-purpose useful computation, would mean running circuits of arbitrary length and depth reliably, by continuously detecting and correcting errors faster than they accumulate — exactly the threshold-theorem condition from Chapter 6. This isn't just more qubits — it requires the full stack this course has built: a code with a workable threshold, fault-tolerant gadgets for every operation including error correction itself, a complete universal gate set including magic-state-distilled T gates, and a decoder fast enough to keep up with continuous syndrome extraction, all operating together, continuously, for as long as the computation runs.

State this directly, as the course's explicit checkpoint: as of now, no quantum computer has run a classically-infeasible, practically useful algorithm end to end in the fault-tolerant regime. The milestones from the last lesson are real and meaningful steps on the path there, but the transition to genuine, useful-scale fault tolerance is the central open engineering challenge of this field — a real, hard, multi-decade problem, with the pieces individually demonstrated at small scale but not yet integrated at the scale Chapter 6's math shows is actually required.

Being able to precisely state what's been demonstrated, what's still needed, and why that gap is measured in orders of magnitude of physical-qubit count, is a genuinely valuable, differentiating skill. Next, the capstone pulls every chapter of this course into one closing worked scenario.
